# The agents layer

This directory adds to the x86-64 [GNU system](../Readme.md) the programs a person uses to work with a coding agent over SSH: each vendor's published build, fetched for the person who builds the image, checked against the digest its vendor publishes, and installed unmodified under its own license. Nothing of a package is committed but its recipe. The layer has twelve packages, GitHub's `gh`, Anthropic's Claude Code, `claude`, Meta's Muse Code, `muse`, OpenAI's Codex, `codex`, Google's Antigravity CLI, `agy`, OpenCode, `opencode`, and ripgrep, `rg`, the search tool the agents run; Node.js with npm and npx, fd, ShellCheck, Ninja and Git LFS supply their developer tools. A package is installed only when the builder names it.

## Use

`GNU_AGENTS` lists the packages the GNU root gets, by the names of their recipes in [`packages/`](packages), or is `all` for every package; it is empty by default. The packages are x86-64 programs, so the variable needs `ARCH=x86_64`:

    make ARCH=x86_64 GNU_AGENTS=gh os-real-gnu-ext2
    make ARCH=x86_64 GNU_AGENTS=all machine

`make ARCH=x86_64 GNU_AGENTS=gh gnu-agents` fetches and stages the packages without building the root. A change to the list, to a recipe or to `fetch_agents.sh` builds the root again; [`mk/gnu-agents.mk`](../../../mk/gnu-agents.mk) has the rules. The release to the installed machine builds with `GNU_AGENTS=all` (`tools/flow/release.sh`), and so does the root `tests/run agents` boots, `os-real-gnu-agents.ext2`.

On the machine each package is a directory of `/opt`, as its vendor published it, with a link to its program in `/usr/bin` and `/bin`. Its page in the manual says how to sign in over SSH and where the credentials are kept: [gh(1)](../../../man/man1/gh.1), [claude(1)](../../../man/man1/claude.1), [codex(1)](../../../man/man1/codex.1), [muse(1)](../../../man/man1/muse.1), [agy(1)](../../../man/man1/agy.1) and [opencode(1)](../../../man/man1/opencode.1); the tools' pages are [rg(1)](../../../man/man1/rg.1), [node(1)](../../../man/man1/node.1) (also npm and npx), [fd(1)](../../../man/man1/fd.1), [shellcheck(1)](../../../man/man1/shellcheck.1), [ninja(1)](../../../man/man1/ninja.1) and [git-lfs(1)](../../../man/man1/git-lfs.1).

After a release has installed the layer on the Lenovo, the owner signs in to each program there over SSH, as an ordinary account and as its page says: `claude auth login`, `codex login --device-auth`, `muse login`, `gh auth login`, for Antigravity CLI its first session, `agy`, which offers Google OAuth, and for OpenCode `opencode auth login openai --method chatgpt-headless`. The acceptance then runs from the owner's computer, in a clone of this tree:

    sh tests/system/accept/agents_accept.sh lenovo USER

USER is the account signed in to, reached by ssh's own key or the one `RACH2_ACCEPT_KEY` names; the machine is at 192.168.0.106 unless a third argument or `RACH2_MACHINE_ADDRESS` names another address, and `RACH2_ACCEPT_AGENTS` may name fewer agents than `claude codex agy muse opencode`. For each agent the script makes a disposable repository, `~/rach2-accept/AGENT`, and in the agent's screen, in tmux over SSH, asks it to read the repository's notes, change a file, run the repository's test and commit, then cancels a turn with Escape, pressed twice for OpenCode, which asks for a second, resizes the terminal, drops and makes again the SSH connection, and reopens the conversation; OpenCode, which runs there with `--standalone`, must then leave no process of its program but those the account had before. Then it reboots the Lenovo and requires each selected program's credential source, version and file, and gh's, to be as they were, and each selected agent to answer one request. A credential source is the file the program's page names, or for OpenCode the secrets of the credential and account records of its database, `~/.local/share/opencode/opencode.db`, which `sqlite3` reads in one transaction, since every session writes the database and the file's digest would change with the sessions it stores. Only the selected programs' sources are required and scanned for strings in the log. The script prints a line for each step and ends with `agents-accept: PASS` or `agents-accept: FAIL (N)`; its log, `build/images/agents-accept-lenovo.log`, has the screens and answers it read, each passed first through a filter on the machine that replaces every string of a credential source, and the script checks there that the log has none of them. [`agents_accept.sh`](../../../tests/system/accept/agents_accept.sh) describes each step in its header.

A package keeps its vendor's license, which the recipe names in `LICENSE` and installs beside the program; `NOTICES` lists those files, and the stage fails without them. Meta publishes no license file for Muse Code, so its recipe writes `/opt/muse/TERMS`, which names the terms and gives their address. Google publishes no license file with `agy` either, so its recipe writes `/opt/agy/TERMS`, which names the three documents that govern its use: the Google Terms of Service, the [Google Antigravity Additional Terms of Service](https://antigravity.google/terms) and the Google Privacy Policy. Claude Code is proprietary: the recipe fetches it for the person who builds the image, and nothing of it is redistributed. Codex's package has the licenses of its voice libraries but not OpenAI's own or those of its other helpers, so its recipe fetches OpenAI's license and notice and bubblewrap's license from the Codex sources at the release's tag, ripgrep's from its tag 15.2.0 and zsh's from the commit the release builds, each pinned by its SHA-256. ripgrep's tarball has its own `COPYING`, `LICENSE-MIT` and `UNLICENSE`, the same files as those Codex's recipe pins, and its recipe installs them as they are. OpenCode's tarball has only the program, so its recipe fetches the repository's `LICENSE` at the release's tag, pinned by its SHA-256. The recipes and `fetch_agents.sh` are in-house.

## Design

### Recipes

A recipe, `packages/NAME.sh`, is a shell fragment that [`fetch_agents.sh`](fetch_agents.sh) reads in a shell of its own. Its header comment says what the program is, where it comes from and how it is pinned. It sets:

* `VERSION`, the version the vendor published.
* `LICENSE`, the license's short name.
* `FILES`, one line for each download: the name it is kept under, its URL, and its digest as the vendor publishes it, `sha256:HEX` or `sha512:HEX`.
* `NOTICES`, the license and notice files, as paths in the stage.

It defines `package_stage DIR`, which lays the package out under `DIR` as the root has it, taking each download through `fetched NAME`. It may define `package_verify`, which checks the vendor's signature on a download, and `package_check DIR`, which runs the staged program on the build host. Both may write in `SCRATCH`, an empty directory of the package's own, which the program may take as its home.

### Developer tools

Node's complete official archive is under `/opt/node`. Its `bin/npm` and `bin/npx` keep their relative links into `lib/node_modules/npm`, and `/usr/bin/node`, `/usr/bin/npm` and `/usr/bin/npx` link to those names. Node uses glibc and GCC's C++ and atomic runtime libraries of the GNU root. Its `LICENSE` includes the licenses of its dependencies; npm has its own `LICENSE` with Artistic-2.0 and dependency notices. The build runs Node, npm and npx's version commands with this archive's Node and a scratch home and cache. On the machine a user may set npm's global prefix to a writable directory, such as `~/.local`; the root does not configure npm for them.

fd is the author's static musl build, ShellCheck a static Linux build, and Git LFS a static Go build. Ninja is the project's Linux build. Each stays under its package's `/opt` directory, with its license beside it and its command linked in `/usr/bin`; the image adds the `/bin` link. ShellCheck, Ninja and Git LFS do not include their own license file in the binary archive, so their recipes fetch one from the same source tag and pin it by SHA-256. Upstream manuals and completions stay with each archive; the shell does not load completions. The in-house manual pages describe the installed commands. No recipe runs `git lfs install` or changes a user's settings.

### Fetching and staging

`fetch_agents.sh NAME...` downloads each file of `FILES` once into `../downloads/agents/NAME/`, which Git ignores, and checks it against its digest each time `fetched` names it, so a download is checked again at every use; a file with another digest is removed and refused. It then makes `SCRATCH`, runs `package_verify`, stages the package from nothing into `agents/NAME/` of the layer's build tree, `build/x86_64/vendor/gnu/agents/NAME/`, checks that each of `NOTICES` is there, runs `package_check`, and removes `SCRATCH`. In the arm64 tooling machine, where QEMU's user-mode emulator runs the staged programs with the toolchain's sysroot as `QEMU_LD_PREFIX`, `package_check` runs with the toolchain's `cross/x86_64-rach2-linux-gnu/lib` on `LD_LIBRARY_PATH`, since the sysroot has glibc but not GCC's runtime libraries, libstdc++, libgcc_s and libatomic, which Ninja and Node.js need. Make runs it behind a stamp for each package, `agents/NAME.stamp`.

`fetch_agents.sh -f NAME FILE` fetches and checks the one download `FILE` of the package `NAME` in the same way, prints its path and stages nothing. It runs on any host, whatever `RACH2_ARCH` says. The `codex-exec` row takes Codex's package through it, since on a Mac the layer builds in etude's tooling machine, which keeps its downloads on the layer's build disk, and the host's tree has none.

### Installing

[`install_root.sh`](../install_root.sh) copies each stage that `GNU_AGENTS` names into the root after the Chromium packages, and refuses a file the root already has, as it does for every part of the layer. Its later steps give each program of `/usr/bin` its name in `/bin`.

### gh

`gh` is a static Go executable and needs no library of the root. Under `/opt/gh` it has `bin/gh`, its manual pages in `share/man/man1` and `LICENSE`. Measured on Linux, it starts no other process for `--version`, `auth status` or `api`. It writes its settings to `~/.config/gh`, and a device identifier and the state of its update check to `~/.local/state/gh`. Before a request it asks the Secret Service of the D-Bus session bus for a stored token, at the address `DBUS_SESSION_BUS_ADDRESS` gives or at `/run/user/UID/bus`, and reads the token from `~/.config/gh/hosts.yml` where there is none. It talks to `api.github.com` and `github.com`, or to the host `GH_HOST` names, whose API it reaches at `https://HOST/api/v3/`, and trusts the certificate authorities of `/etc/ssl/certs`, with those of the file `SSL_CERT_FILE` names. It does not update itself: on a terminal it checks GitHub for a newer release once a day and prints a notice, which `GH_NO_UPDATE_NOTIFIER` turns off. Its telemetry, on by default, is turned off by `gh config set telemetry disabled` or `GH_TELEMETRY=false`.

### claude

Claude Code is one executable of 257 MB, a program for Bun, a JavaScript runtime, with the runtime and its scripts in the file. Under `/opt/claude` it has `bin/claude` and `LICENSE.md`, and the recipe adds the managed settings, `/etc/claude-code/managed-settings.json`, which come before every other setting. Anthropic's setup page describes the signed manifest that `package_verify` checks: the key is published armored, `gpgv` reads it as a binary keyring, which is the armor's base64 body, and the fingerprint of the key that made the signature is the last field of `gpgv`'s `VALIDSIG` status line. The binary must then have the SHA-256 that the manifest lists under `platforms.linux-x64.checksum`.

What follows was measured with 2.1.296 on the testing host, Ubuntu under WSL 2, under `strace` and behind a proxy that logged each request, in a fresh home. Under WSL every command also runs Windows' `reg.exe` to read Anthropic's policy keys in the registry, which it does not do where there is no WSL.

* Libraries: it links against glibc 2.26 or later, `libc.so.6`, `libm.so.6`, `libpthread.so.0`, `libdl.so.2`, `librt.so.1` and `ld-linux-x86-64.so.2`, which the GNU root has. It reads the certificate authorities of `/etc/ssl/cert.pem` and `/etc/ssl/certs`, with those of the file `NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS` names.
* Processes: `--version`, `--help` and `auth status` start none, nor does `update` with the managed settings. A session runs `/bin/bash -c -l` once to save the login shell's environment, and each command of its Bash tool as `/bin/bash -c` with that saved environment; it runs `git` on the repository, its own file under the name `rg` for ripgrep, which it has built in, `uname`, and `gh auth token` and a `gh issue list` of the user's closed issues on `anthropics/claude-code` when the path finds `gh`. `claude doctor`, and `claude update` without the managed settings, run `npm -g config get prefix` where the path finds `npm`.
* Files: `--version` and `--help` write nothing. The other commands, `auth status` among them, write `~/.claude.json`, its settings and the state of each project, through a temporary file and a rename under the lock `~/.claude.json.lock`, and `~/.claude/`: `sessions/`, `backups/`, `cache/`, `projects/` with the transcripts, `plugins/` with Anthropic's catalog of plugins, and `.credentials.json`, mode 0600, after a sign-in. `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` names another directory for `~/.claude`. A session also makes `claude-UID/` and `cc-socks/`, with a socket for each session, under `TMPDIR`, or `/tmp`.
* Hosts: the model's requests go to `api.anthropic.com`, or to `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL`. A session with no sign-in and the settings as the vendor ships them also reached `api.anthropic.com` for its start-up settings, the list of MCP servers, feature flags and usage events; `http-intake.logs.us5.datadoghq.com` for its logs; `downloads.claude.ai` for its update, `/claude-code-releases/latest` and then the new version's `manifest.json` and binary, and for the catalog of plugins; `raw.githubusercontent.com` for the change log of `anthropics/claude-code`; and, at the first start, `platform.claude.com`. `claude auth login` gives an address at `claude.com/cai/oauth/authorize` to open in a browser. It takes a proxy from `HTTPS_PROXY`.
* Updates: as shipped, a session fetches `latest` from `downloads.claude.ai` at its start and installs a newer version into `~/.local/share/claude/versions/` for the next start, and `claude update` and `claude install` do the same on demand. With `DISABLE_UPDATES` set to 1 in the managed settings, as the recipe writes them, a session fetched no release, and `claude update` and `claude install` printed `Updates are disabled by your administrator` and exited with status 0 without fetching a release, at once with no network as well; `claude doctor` reports `Auto-updates: disabled (set by env: DISABLE_UPDATES)`. `DISABLE_AUTOUPDATER` alone stops only the background update.
* Telemetry: usage events go to `api.anthropic.com/api/event_logging/`, logs to Datadog, and feature flags come from `api.anthropic.com/api/eval/`; `DISABLE_TELEMETRY=1` stopped all three. `CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_NONESSENTIAL_TRAFFIC=1` stopped every request of the session but the download of the catalog of plugins, which `CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_OFFICIAL_MARKETPLACE_AUTOINSTALL=1` stopped too. The recipe sets neither; [claude(1)](../../../man/man1/claude.1) gives the settings to the person who uses it.
* Sandbox: off, as Anthropic ships it, until a person's settings set `sandbox.enabled`. Then each command of the Bash tool runs under `/usr/bin/bwrap`, in a network namespace of its own, with the files outside the working directory read-only and a seccomp filter of Claude Code's own; its requests leave only through Claude Code's proxy, which `/usr/bin/socat` joins to the namespace's loopback interface at port 3128, and which allows only the hosts the settings list. Measured on Rach2 in QEMU with `failIfUnavailable` set, so that a sandbox that could not start would have stopped the command: the command could not write `/etc`, `/proc/self/status` showed the filter, and its request to a host the settings did not list got the proxy's 403.

### muse

Muse Code is one static executable of 376 MB, which needs no library of the root. Meta's installer, `https://dev.meta.ai/install.sh`, puts a launcher script at `~/.local/bin/muse`. The launcher reads the channel manifest, `https://api.meta.ai/muse-code/channels/muse-stable`, for the current version and its release manifest, downloads the file that manifest lists for the platform, checks its size and SHA-256, keeps it beside itself as `muse-bin-VERSION` and runs it. Each time it starts it looks for a newer launcher and a newer version, at most once an hour, and installs them in the background; `MUSE_NO_AUTO_UPDATE=1` turns that off. The program has no update code of its own, so the layer installs it without the launcher, and it stays at the version the recipe pins.

Measured on Linux, `--version` and `--help` start no other process and write no file. Its screen asks whether to trust the directory it starts in, and writes the answer to `~/.config/muse/trust.json`. It makes `~/.local/share/muse`, with a SQLite index of its sessions, the sessions, its bundled skills and plugins and a log of each start, and makes and removes scratch directories under `TMPDIR` or `/tmp`. To learn whether its sandbox works it runs `/usr/bin/bwrap`, where there is one, and itself as `muse __tbh_internal_bwrap`, its own copy of bubblewrap; it also reads `/etc/ssh/ssh_config`. The sandbox, on as Meta ships it, runs each shell command under that copy with the files outside the workspace read-only; measured on Rach2 in QEMU, a command of `muse exec` could not write `/etc` and wrote the workspace. With no credential it offers two sign-ins: by browser, a device code that `auth.meta.com` confirms, for which it runs `xdg-open` on the address and also prints it, or by a Model API key typed in. A key in `META_API_KEY` signs it in without either and takes priority over a stored credential, which it keeps in `~/.config/muse/auth.json`. Its settings are `~/.config/muse/settings.json`, where `"telemetry": {"enabled": false}` turns off its telemetry. It talks to `api.meta.ai` and `auth.meta.com`, or to the server `--base-url` names, and trusts as well the certificate authority whose file the setting `endpoint_transport.ca_bundle` names.

### codex

Codex is a static Rust executable built for musl. Under `/opt/codex` it has the files of OpenAI's package as the release has them: `bin/codex`, `bin/codex-code-mode-host`, `codex-path/rg`, `codex-resources/bwrap`, `codex-resources/zsh/bin/zsh`, the voice host with its libraries in `codex-resources/voice`, and `codex-package.json`, which names the program and the two directories. Codex finds its helpers from the path of its own program, which it reads from `/proc/self/exe`, so `/usr/bin/codex` is a link to `/opt/codex/bin/codex`. Its zsh and its voice host link against glibc, which the root has. Beside the package are `LICENSE`, `NOTICE` and `licenses/`, with the licenses of ripgrep, bubblewrap and zsh.

Codex reads its settings from its system configuration file, `/etc/codex/config.toml`, which the recipe writes, then from `~/.codex/config.toml` and the command line, each over the one before. It writes its state to `~/.codex`, or to the directory `CODEX_HOME` names: its settings, an installation identifier, SQLite databases of its sessions and logs, the credentials of a sign-in in `auth.json`, and in `tmp/arg0` links to its own program under the names of the commands it runs as, such as `apply_patch`, which it does not make in a home under `/tmp`. It talks to `api.openai.com` with an API key, and to `chatgpt.com` and `auth.openai.com` with a ChatGPT sign-in. With an API key too, a session fetches the catalog of plugins as it starts and again as it ends: `/backend-api/plugins/featured` and `/backend-api/plugins/export/curated` from `chatgpt.com`, and `/repos/openai/plugins` from `api.github.com`; the feature `plugins`, which `codex features disable plugins` turns off, makes all three. As it starts, its screen also fetches a notice to show, `/openai/codex/main/announcement_tip.toml` from `raw.githubusercontent.com`, which `tui.show_tooltips = false` does not stop. Codex trusts the system's certificate authorities, with those of the file `CODEX_CA_CERTIFICATE` names, or `SSL_CERT_FILE` where it is unset.

Measured on Linux, offline, with Codex's screen showing its sign-in menu in tmux, Codex 0.162.1 with no settings is three processes. The screen, `/opt/codex/bin/codex`, has 110 MB resident. Before it draws, it copies the whole package, 430 MB, to `~/.codex/packages/app-server-daemon/releases/0.162.1-x86_64-unknown-linux-musl` and starts two processes from the copy: the shared server, `codex app-server --listen unix:// --analytics-default-enabled --managed-daemon`, 245 MB, which runs the sessions for every screen of the user and for `codex agents`; and its updater, `codex app-server daemon pid-update-loop`, 190 MB, which from five minutes after it starts runs `https://chatgpt.com/codex/install.sh` to install a newer release beside the copy and restarts the server from it. Both outlive the screen. The recipe's settings make it one process of 120 MB and no copy:

* `features.daemon_auto_start = false`, a feature that `codex features list` shows and `codex features disable` sets, starts no server, so the screen runs its sessions in its own process. The documented option `--no-daemon` does the same for one run, and so does a `-c` option on the command line other than a few feature switches. `check_for_update_on_startup = false` alone leaves all three processes.
* `check_for_update_on_startup = false` keeps the screen from asking `api.github.com` for the latest release when it starts, and from offering an update. Codex counts `/opt/codex` as a local build, which it does not update in any case.

The sandbox is left as shipped. Codex runs each command the model asks for under the bundled bubblewrap, which it runs through `/proc/self/fd/N`, with a seccomp filter that refuses the network; `sandbox_mode`, or `--sandbox` for one run, chooses what the command may write, and `danger-full-access` runs it with no sandbox. Measured on Rach2 in QEMU with `codex sandbox`, `read-only`, the default of `codex exec`, refused a write anywhere, `workspace-write` allowed one in the working directory alone, and both refused the command a socket.

### agy

`agy` is Google's build of Antigravity CLI, a dynamically linked x86-64 executable for glibc of 220,553,472 bytes, written in Go with BoringCrypto. It needs `libc.so.6`, `libpthread.so.0`, `libdl.so.2`, `libm.so.6`, `librt.so.1` and `libresolv.so.2`, which the root has. Under `/opt/agy` it has `bin/agy`, the one file of Google's tarball, `antigravity`, under the name Google's installer gives it, and `TERMS`. The installer also runs `agy install`, which adds the program's directory to the shell's startup files; the recipe does not, since `/usr/bin` has the link.

Measured on Linux, it starts no other process for `--version`, `--help` or its screen up to the sign-in, and a session run with `-p` leaves none behind. `--version` and `--help` write nothing. Its first session writes about 17 MB to `~/.gemini/antigravity-cli/`, with its settings, conversations, logs, cache and an installation identifier, and to `~/.gemini/config/`, with its projects. Among them are helpers it unpacks from itself into `~/.gemini/antigravity-cli/bin/`: `webm_encoder`, an executable whose interpreter is `/usr/grte/v5/lib64/ld-linux-x86-64.so.2`, a path that Debian, Ubuntu and this root lack, and, after a session that runs a command, `agentapi`, a shell script. It trusts the certificate authorities of `/etc/ssl/certs`, or in their place those of the file `SSL_CERT_FILE` names, as Go's runtime does. Its `run_command` sends a command to the background at most 10 seconds after it starts, whatever `WaitMsBeforeAsync` the model gives; the turn then goes on, and Escape no longer ends the command.

A session that is not signed in offers two ways to sign in: Google OAuth, for a Google account, and a Google Cloud project. With Google OAuth it prints the address of Google's sign-in page and waits for the code the page shows once the person has signed in, so a machine without a browser signs in from any other computer. It keeps the token in the Secret Service of the D-Bus session bus where one answers, and otherwise in `~/.gemini/antigravity-cli/antigravity-oauth-token`. With `"modelProvider": "gemini"` in `~/.gemini/antigravity-cli/settings.json` and a key in `GEMINI_API_KEY` it needs no sign-in and sends its requests to the Gemini API, or to the server that `GOOGLE_GEMINI_BASE_URL` names.

Its updater runs in the background and replaces the program with Google's newest release. It first creates a file in the program's directory, and stops when it cannot, as an ordinary user cannot write `/opt/agy/bin`. `AGY_CLI_DISABLE_AUTO_UPDATE=true`, the setting Google documents, turns it off: the stage's `/etc/profile.d/agy.sh` sets it, and the root's `/etc/profile` reads that directory, so every login shell has it. A command that `ssh` runs without a login shell does not.

Each session sends Google usage events and asks a server for feature flags. Measured on Linux, a session of `-p` posts about 62 kB in two requests to `https://play.googleapis.com/log`, and registers with `antigravity-unleash.goog`, a server of the Unleash feature-flag protocol, and fetches the flags from it. Google documents `"enableTelemetry": false` in `~/.gemini/antigravity-cli/settings.json` as the setting that turns metrics off, but version 1.4.0 writes the file again without that member at each start, headless or in its screen, and sends the same events whether it is false, true or absent. Google documents no other setting that stops either. With neither server reachable, or with each answering 404, the program works on as before.

### ripgrep

`rg` is a static Rust executable for musl, 5,408,904 bytes, with PCRE2 10.45 and its JIT built in, and needs no library of the root. Under `/opt/ripgrep` it has the files of the release's tarball as published: `rg`, the licenses, `README.md`, `doc/` with the release's manual page `rg.1` and its guide, FAQ and change log, and `complete/` with completions for bash, fish, zsh and PowerShell, which no shell of the root loads. `/usr/bin/rg` links to the program. Claude Code and Codex do not run it: Claude Code runs its own file under the name `rg`, and Codex the copy in its package, `codex-path/rg`, the same version.

Measured on Linux under `strace`, `--version` starts no other process and writes no file. A search writes no file and makes no connection. It reads `~/.gitconfig` for `core.excludesFile`, and the ignore files of the directories it searches and of those above them; it counts the processors it may run on with `sched_getaffinity` and the `cpu.max` of its cgroup under `/sys/fs/cgroup`, which Rach2 does not have, and chooses from that count how many threads to search with. Only `-z`, which runs the decompressor the path finds, such as `gzip -d -c`, and `--pre`, which runs the command it names, start a process. In QEMU on Rach2, `rg --version`, a search of `/usr/share` and `/usr/include` in two threads, `-z` on a gzip file and `-P` behave as on Linux.

### opencode

OpenCode is one executable of 252,713,136 bytes, a program for Bun with the runtime, its scripts and its native libraries in the file. The release's `linux-x64-baseline` build, which needs no AVX2, is in 2.2.5 the same file as its `linux-x64` build. Under `/opt/opencode` it has `bin/opencode`, the one file of the tarball, and `LICENSE`; `/etc/profile.d/opencode.sh` sets `OPENCODE_DISABLE_AUTOUPDATE=1` for every login shell. Version 2 runs its sessions in a background service, which the recipe leaves as the project ships it.

What follows was measured with 2.2.5 on the testing host, Ubuntu under WSL 2, under `strace`, in a fresh home.

* Libraries: it links against glibc, `libc.so.6`, `libm.so.6`, `libpthread.so.0`, `libdl.so.2` and `ld-linux-x86-64.so.2`. At each start Bun writes native libraries out of the file into `TMPDIR`, or `/tmp`, as `.bun-UID-HASH.so` or `.node`, mode 0600, and leaves them there: `libopentui.so`, 5 MB, which draws the screen, at every start, `--version` among them; and in a session FFF's file finder, 13 MB, and `watcher.node`, the file watcher, which also needs `libstdc++.so.6` and `libgcc_s.so.1`, which the root's runtime has.
* Processes: `--version` and `--help` start none. A command that needs a session, the screen, `run`, `auth` and `models` among them, connects to the user's background service and starts it as `opencode serve --service` when none runs. The service listens on a port of 127.0.0.1, whose address and process it writes to `~/.local/state/opencode/service.json`, takes the password in `~/.config/opencode/service.json`, mode 0600, and outlives the client until `opencode service stop`. With `--standalone` the client starts a private server instead, `opencode serve --stdio --port 0`, which ends with it and leaves no process. The server runs `git` in the directory to find the repository, its remote and its branch: `rev-parse`, `remote`, `remote get-url origin` and `symbolic-ref`.
* Files: it keeps its files under the XDG base directories, `~/.local/share/opencode`, `~/.config/opencode`, `~/.local/state/opencode` and `~/.cache/opencode`, which `XDG_DATA_HOME` and the others move. `--version` writes its log, `~/.local/share/opencode/log/opencode.log`. A session writes `~/.local/share/opencode/opencode.db`, a SQLite database in WAL mode with mode 0600, which holds the sessions and every credential, API keys in the table `credential` and the tokens of OpenCode's console in `account`, all in plain text; `OPENCODE_DB` names another file. `opencode auth export` prints the credentials as JSON and `opencode auth import` reads them back.
* Sign-in: `opencode auth login` connects an integration by one of its methods. Over SSH, ChatGPT signs in by a device code with `--method chatgpt-headless`, which prints `https://auth.openai.com/codex/device` and a code, and OpenCode's console with `--method device`, which prints an address at `https://opencode.ai/console/device`; the method `Sign in with ChatGPT` waits for a browser on this machine's loopback interface. A provider's key is typed on the terminal, or taken unstored from its variable, such as `OPENAI_API_KEY`. OpenCode's own provider lists a few free models with no sign-in.
* Updates: as shipped, the client asks `opencode.ai` at each start for a newer release and reports one; `OPENCODE_DISABLE_AUTOUPDATE` set to 1 or true skips the check. `opencode upgrade` installs by the method it finds the program was installed with: a program at `~/.opencode/bin/opencode` by the project's installer, else Homebrew, winget or a JavaScript package manager. It finds none for `/opt/opencode`, and fails with `Could not detect the installation method`.
* Search: the tools `grep` and `glob` run ripgrep, the first `rg` on the path; with none there OpenCode downloads ripgrep's release from GitHub and checks its SHA-256. FFF, a file finder in Rust, answers the server's search for file names, `/api/fs/find`, which the screen's `@` completion asks. In a git tree the server starts it at once: it scans and watches the tree with inotify on threads of its own, `fff-bg-N`, `fff-git-status` and `fff-watcher-own`, and holds its index in memory. OpenCode gives it no path for its frecency or history database, so FFF opens no LMDB. `OPENCODE_DISABLE_FFF=1` leaves FFF out, and the server then lists the tree with ripgrep.
* Sandbox: OpenCode has none. The commands the model asks for and the edits it makes run with the user's rights; its permission settings decide which it asks about first, and `--auto` approves every request they do not deny.

## Building

The layer builds where the rest of the GNU layer does ([its Readme](../Readme.md#building)), on an x86-64 Linux host or in etude's tooling machine, with access to each vendor's download site. Besides the tools the [GNU layer](../Readme.md#building) lists it needs `sha512sum`, or `shasum`, for a package pinned by SHA-512, and `gpgv` and `base64` for Claude Code's signature. The check of Codex's signature also needs access to Sigstore's repository of its trusted root, `tuf-repo-cdn.sigstore.dev`, from which `cosign` fetches the root into a scratch home. Codex's downloads are 300 MB, its stage 440 MB.

## Updating

To update a package, take the new version's digest from the list its vendor publishes, verifying the list's signature where the vendor signs it, and set `VERSION` and the digest in the recipe. For Claude Code, fetch the new release's `manifest.json` and `manifest.json.sig`, verify the signature by [Anthropic's procedure](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/setup#verify-the-manifest-signature) with the key whose fingerprint is `FINGERPRINT`, and set the binary's digest from the manifest's `linux-x64` entry, the digests of the manifest and its signature, and the npm package's `dist.integrity` from `https://registry.npmjs.org/@anthropic-ai/claude-code/VERSION`, decoded from base64 to hex. A new key changes `FINGERPRINT` only after its fingerprint is checked against the setup page. For ripgrep it is the line of the tarball's own `.sha256` file, which matches the digest the release's API gives for the asset. For Codex these are the line of `codex-package_SHA256SUMS` for the package and the digests the release's API lists for the package's `.sigstore` bundle; the bundle's certificate must name the release workflow of the new tag, which `package_verify` requires. The license files come again from the new tag, and from the ripgrep version and the zsh commit that the tag's `scripts/codex_package/rg` and `.github/workflows/rust-release-zsh.yml` name. OpenCode publishes several releases a day, so its pin falls behind fast; move it at the start of a milestone, not within one. Its versions come from the releases `vVERSION` of `anomalyco/opencode` on GitHub, whose `SHA256SUMS` gives the line for `opencode-linux-x64-baseline.tar.gz`, and the license's digest from `LICENSE` at the new tag. The project's installer, `https://opencode.ai/install`, installs only the 1.x line, which the project still releases beside 2.x, as 1.19.5. Then update the package's row in the table above, its page in the manual and what its row in `tests/system/agents/` expects, among them, for OpenCode, the name, length and offset in the program of each library Bun writes into TMPDIR, and run `ARCH=x86_64 tests/run agents`.

A new package is a recipe in `packages/`, a row in `tests/system/agents/`, with a script for the fake server where the row talks to the vendor's service, a page in [`man/`](../../../man/Readme.md), a line in the table above and a section of Design that records what the program needs.

## Limits

* The packages are x86-64 programs, and the layer installs them only in the x86-64 GNU root.
* Claude Code's sandbox is off as shipped, and its shell commands run with the user's own rights until a person's settings turn it on.
* A sandbox's network namespace has IPv4 on its loopback interface alone, so a sandboxed command reaches no IPv6 address, `::1` among them, and a `/dev/pts` mounted in it is the machine's own terminals, not a new set ([vfs.Readme.md](../../../rach2/sys/fs/vfs.Readme.md)).
* GitHub signs no file of `gh`'s release. Its build provenance attestations are checked by `gh attestation verify`, which needs a sign-in, so the recipe pins the digest the checksums file lists.
* Meta signs neither manifest of Muse Code's release, so the recipe pins the digest the release manifest lists. Meta's terms let the person who fetched the program install and use it, and forbid giving it to anyone else: a root built with `muse` is not to be given away.
* OpenCode has no sandbox at all: the model's commands run as the user who runs it, and with `--auto` without asking.
* OpenCode signs no file of its release, so the recipe pins the digest `SHA256SUMS` lists, as it does for `gh`.
* OpenCode's background service, which the screen and `run` start unless given `--standalone`, outlives them until `opencode service stop` or a reboot, and keeps its memory meanwhile.
* OpenCode leaves the native libraries that Bun writes out at each start in `TMPDIR`.
* `/etc/profile.d/opencode.sh`, which turns off OpenCode's update check, is read only by a login shell, as Antigravity CLI's is.

## Tests

The host scripts wait for SSH and session state without setting completion deadlines. Etude supervises each enclosing step with the existing bounds and watchdog of [`machine.agents`](../../../tests/cases/machine.agents.json), [`machine.agentsaccept`](../../../tests/cases/machine.agentsaccept.json) and [`machine.fakeapi`](../../../tests/cases/machine.fakeapi.json). Its case manifests and the machine's history determine those bounds. The Lenovo acceptance waits for the same events.

`fetch_agents.sh` runs each recipe's `package_check` on the build host when it stages the package. On a build host that is not x86, such as etude's arm64 tooling machine on a Mac, the programs run through QEMU's user-mode emulator, under which Claude Code, a program of Bun's, aborts at its start, so its check is not run there. `ARCH=x86_64 tests/run agents` boots a private copy of `os-real-gnu-agents.ext2` for each row, with 4 GiB of memory on a network whose only route out is to the fake API server on the host ([`tests/system/fakeapi/`](../../../tests/system/fakeapi/Readme.md)), and runs the rows of [`tests/system/agents/`](../../../tests/system/agents) over SSH as the test account; [the cases](../../../tests/cases/Readme.md) describe the scenario, row driver and private API services. The `gh` row checks the pinned version, the program the path finds and its license, `gh auth status` with no account signed in, one HTTPS request from `gh api` with no account to openssl's test server on the machine, which `gh` refuses until `SSL_CERT_FILE` names the server's certificate, and `GH_TOKEN=invalid gh api user` against the fake server as `api.github.com`, which answers 401 as GitHub does. The `agy` row checks the pinned version, the program the path finds and its terms, `AGY_CLI_DISABLE_AUTO_UPDATE` in a login shell and `agy --help`; then, in a home of its own and with no route out, it starts `agy` in tmux, requires the menu of ways to sign in, chooses Google OAuth, and requires Google's sign-in address and the prompt for the code, and requires that no process of the program is left once tmux has ended. The `muse` row checks the pinned version, the program the path finds and the terms beside it, `muse --help`, and its screen in tmux, in a home of its own: the question whether to trust the directory, the answer recorded in `trust.json`, the two sign-ins it offers with no credential, and its end, not signed in, at Esc. The `claude` row checks the pinned version, the program the path finds and Anthropic's notice, the first line of `claude --help`, `claude update`, which the managed settings refuse without fetching a release, and the version after it, and `claude auth status` with no account signed in; it needs no network. The `codex` row checks the pinned version, the program the path finds and its license, `codex login status` with no account signed in and `codex exec --help`, then starts Codex in tmux from a home with no `~/.codex` and requires the sign-in menu, with sign-in by a device code, while Codex is one process, run from `/opt/codex/bin/codex`, with no copy in `~/.codex/packages`, and last that `codex features list` says the background server is off. The `worker-session` row runs the worker loop itself, `tools/flow/worker.sh` from a clone of a bare copy of a git repository of the tree's tests and tools as its `origin`, with Claude Code against the fake server and `gh` on the path a stand-in, [`fakegh.py`](../../../tests/system/agents/fakegh.py), that serves one open milestone whose description names the branch `milestone/01-worker`, two Ready tasks #901 and #902, and #903, a subtask of #901. The row first requires that `board.sh next` lists only #901 and #902. The loop takes #901, and its session, playing [`worker-session.json`](../../../tests/system/agents/worker-session.json), commits on `task/901`, closes #903, rebases and pushes HEAD to `milestone/01-worker`, closes #901 with a comment that names the commit, and deletes `task/901` in the clone and on the origin. The loop finds #901 closed and takes #902, whose session commits and pushes `task/902`, comments and hands the task back with `board.sh release`. Once the second session has started the row writes the loop's stop file. The case judges on the host every recorded request against its step with `agent_server verify`, the loop's log, the board, the calls made to `gh`, each session's result and Anthropic's digest of the program with `agent_server worker-proof`, and the origin's master, milestone branch and task branches with the machine's Git.

`ARCH=x86_64 tests/run agentsaccept` runs the acceptance of the Lenovo, under [Use](#use), as one etude machine case per agent: on a private copy of `os-real-gnu-agents.ext2` with 4 GiB of memory, as the test account, with the dummy keys and settings that point every program at the fake API server, whose names the machine's `/etc/hosts` gives. The server plays [`tests/system/accept/agents/AGENT.json`](../../../tests/system/accept/agents) for each program: its `session` while the agent works in its screen, the exchange of the agents suite's rows on the shared fixture, followed by a turn that runs `sleep 600`, and its `after` for the request after the reboot. The steps and their checks are those on the Lenovo, and each program's script must pass as well, every step played and no request it does not have. Each agent cancels a running command with Escape; Codex leaves the command running in a background terminal, which its `/stop` ends. Since Antigravity CLI sends the command to the background after 10 seconds, its case presses Escape from the client machine a second after the client's screen shows `Running (sleep 600)`, and a watcher started on the machine before the request, `guest.sh watch`, proves that the process ran; for the other agents the case finds the process on the machine first. Claude Code reopens with `--continue`, Codex with `resume --last`, Antigravity CLI with `--continue` and Muse Code with `resume --last`, and none asks the model anything to show the conversation again.

The `muse` row then runs `muse exec --yolo` in a fresh home and a clone of the shared fixture: read `notes.txt`, run `check.sh`, edit `greeting.txt` and commit. The server checks each tool result before the next turn. The host checks the returned file, committed tree, author, two commits and clean work tree. It also checks the binary's digest before and after each session, with an empty environment except the test settings.

The headless row uses the shared [Responses script](../../../tests/system/fakeapi/muse.json). The `agentsaccept` case covers the interactive exchange, including its startup requests, command cancellation and the reopened conversation. The separate screen rows are removed; their interactive operations remain in acceptance and their edit-and-commit exchanges remain in the headless rows.

Measured on the testing host in a 4096 MiB x86-64 guest, with TCG and two processors, on Muse Code's pinned version above. The digest check caches the binary's file before the session. Free frames are sampled from `/proc/vmstat` once a second; a frame is 4096 bytes. The fall is from the first sample to the smallest. These measurements set no pass criterion.

| Mode | Session (s) | Minimum sampled free frames | Fall from start (KiB) |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| `exec` | 43 | 894906 | 117420 |
| `tmux` | 52 | 889516 | 233460 |

The host samples request arrival every 0.1 s. Each interval below starts at the request that selects the tool and ends at the request containing its result, including the HTTPS exchange and tool execution.

The `claude-print` row has Claude Code play the exchange of [`claude-session.json`](../../../tests/system/fakeapi/claude-session.json) as the test account with `claude -p`, in a fresh home and the fixture repository. The retained `agentsaccept` case answers the first-start questions in the interactive screen and checks repository work, cancellation, resizing, reconnecting and conversation resume. Asked to, Claude Code reads the fixture, runs a command, edits the file and commits it with git, and the fake server checks each tool result before it answers. The case judges the returned file and commit and every recorded request on the host, and requires Anthropic's digest of the program before and after the session. The session's environment names the fake server as the gateway, `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL`; every host name Claude Code reaches as shipped, listed under [claude](#claude), is the fake server's too, so a request to any of them that the script does not have fails the row, and the machine has no route anywhere else. While a session runs, the row requires the process to run `/opt/claude/bin/claude` with no `LD_` variable in its environment, no `/etc/ld.so.preload`, and no file mapped but the program, the six libraries of glibc it links against and the linker's cache, `/etc/ld.so.cache`.

The intervals are measured as for Muse Code. The first two turns are messages on the WebSocket, and the check's interval includes the WebSocket the server refuses and Codex's change to HTTPS.

| Mode | Read (s) | Check (s) | Edit (s) | Check and commit (s) |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| `codex exec` | 0.9 | 1.2 | 0.5 | 1.7 |
| screen | 1.1 | 1.1 | 0.3 | 1.4 |

The `opencode` row checks the pinned version, the program the path finds and its license, and ripgrep on the path, which OpenCode's search tools run. It then starts `opencode serve` on a port of the loopback interface, in a home and a TMPDIR of its own, and requires the server to map no file but the program, glibc, the C++ runtime, its database's shared memory and the three libraries Bun writes out of the program into TMPDIR, libopentui, FFF and the file watcher, each of which must be byte for byte the slice of the pinned program that the row's table gives. Two servers share the home, and so its SQLite database in WAL mode, and search a git tree at once through `/api/fs/find`, which FFF answers; one is killed with SIGKILL, and the other and a third started after it must still find the tree's files. FFF opens no LMDB, as [opencode](#opencode) says, and the row requires that none exists. A server started in a git tree of more directories than `fs.inotify.max_user_watches` must still find a file in it, and once every server has ended a new inotify instance of the account must add exactly that many watches before ENOSPC, so that no server left one held. Last, the row samples the memory of `opencode session list --standalone` and of its private server and the time each takes to start, requires that it leaves no process, and that `opencode session list` without `--standalone` leaves the background service, one process, recorded in `~/.local/state/opencode/service.json`, which `opencode service stop` ends, removing the record. It lists sessions, not models, since the server answers the list of models only once its plugins are active and gives up after 5 seconds with `Location plugins did not finish activating`, less than they take to start under QEMU without acceleration. A native run makes the row's tree itself.

The `opencode-run` row has OpenCode play the exchange of [`opencode.json`](../../../tests/system/fakeapi/opencode.json) as the test account with `opencode run --standalone --auto`, in a fresh home and a clone of the shared fixture, with FFF on. Asked to, OpenCode reads `notes.txt` with `read`, searches the tree with `grep`, which runs ripgrep, runs `check.sh` with `shell`, edits `greeting.txt` with `patch`, runs `check.sh` again and commits, and the fake server checks each tool result before it answers. OpenCode reaches the server as its provider `openai`, whose `baseURL` and dummy key the home's `opencode.json` sets, and trusts the test authority through `NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS`. It first asks for a WebSocket, which the server refuses with 426, and goes on over HTTPS. `--title` names the session, so that OpenCode asks the model for no title, and `OPENCODE_DISABLE_MODELS_FETCH=1` keeps it from fetching the list of models from `models.dev`. `api.openai.com`, `models.dev` and `opencode.ai` are the fake server's names too, so a request to any of them fails the row, and the machine has no route anywhere else. While the last answer is held, the row requires the client and its private server, `opencode serve --stdio`, each to map no file but those the `opencode` row allows, and once the session has ended no process of the program may be left. The case judges the returned file and commit and every recorded request, with OpenCode's user agent, on the host, and requires before and after the session the digest of `opencode` in the pinned tarball, which the rule of `mk/gnu-agents.mk` writes to `build/tests/cases/machine/opencode.sha256`.
